sections.title: ISM Sensor Recognition Explained
sections.tabSummary: What automatic sensor recognition actually prevents
body: What automatic sensor recognition actually removes from routine pH calibration.

Every pH sensor has its own calibration history and characteristics, and manually re-entering that information every time a sensor is connected, or worse, using the wrong calibration data with the wrong sensor, is a genuine source of measurement error. That risk grows in a shared lab where sensors get swapped between meters or operators.

SD20's Intelligent Sensor Management (ISM) reads the sensor's own stored data the moment it's connected, calibration history included, so the meter recognizes exactly which sensor is attached and configures itself accordingly, without the operator entering anything manually.

sections.tabSummary: What one sensor covering 0.001 μS/cm to 2000 mS/cm actually removes
body: What one sensor covering 0.001 μS/cm to 2000 mS/cm actually removes from routine testing.

Conductivity spans an enormous range in practice, from ultra-pure water at a few μS/cm to concentrated process solutions in the mS/cm range, and a sensor built for only one end of that scale either loses accuracy or can't measure at all outside its designed band. A lab testing both ends normally needs to switch sensors, or own two meters.

SD30's InLab 731-ISM sensor is built to cover medium and high conductivities across the full 0.001 μS/cm to 2000 mS/cm range on the same instrument, so switching between a low-conductivity water sample and a high-conductivity process solution doesn't mean switching hardware.

body: What running pH and conductivity on one instrument actually saves over two separate meters.

Testing both pH and conductivity on the same sample is common enough in water quality and general QC work that a lab doing it regularly ends up either running two separate meters side by side, or moving one sample between two instruments. Either way, that's two calibration routines, two sets of standards, and two records to keep in sync.

SD23 puts both channels on the identical SevenDirect platform, so calibrating, measuring, and recording both parameters happens through one touchscreen, one guided workflow, and one set of stored results, without either parameter's accuracy being compromised to make room for the other.

body: What pX and ppm actually tell you, and why SD50 reports both.

Ion-selective electrodes measure the concentration of one specific ion in a sample, chloride, fluoride, sodium, and others, but the unit that concentration gets reported in depends on who's reading it. Chemists often work in pX, the negative logarithm of the ion's activity, the same style of unit as pH itself, while a QC report or regulatory spec is more likely to want a direct concentration in mg/L or ppm.
SD50 reports both, with auto-ranging 3- or 4-digit resolution, so a result doesn't need converting by hand to match whichever unit the lab's paperwork actually uses.

sections.title: Pure-Water Conductivity Sensors Explained
sections.tabSummary: Why a generalist probe isn't the right tool at trace conductivity
body: Why a generalist conductivity probe isn't the right tool at the pure-water end of the scale.

A generalist conductivity sensor is built to handle a wide range reasonably well, but "reasonably well" at both ends of a range spanning 0.001 μS/cm to 2000 mS/cm usually means genuine compromises at the extremes. At the low end, in purified or ultra-pure water, a sensor not specifically designed for it can struggle to hold accuracy where the conductivity signal itself is faint.

NF3000's InLab 741 Pro-DES sensor is built specifically for pure water, rather than adapted from a generalist design, which matters most for pharmaceutical water systems, semiconductor rinse water, and any lab where the samples sit consistently at the low, sensitive end of the conductivity scale.

sections.title: LE703 Sensor Range Explained
sections.tabSummary: What "medium to high conductivities" means in practice
body: What "medium to high conductivities" actually means for choosing the right sensor.

Conductivity spans several orders of magnitude in practice, and no single sensor design covers the entire range equally well. LE703, the probe included with FP30-Std, is built specifically for the 10 μS/cm to 200 mS/cm range, medium to high conductivities, which covers most process solutions, buffers, and general laboratory samples.

For genuinely low-conductivity samples, purified or ultra-pure water in the low μS/cm range, a different sensor, such as the LE740 built for 0.01 μS/cm to 500 μS/cm, is the better fit. Choosing the right sensor for the sample's actual conductivity range matters more than the meter itself once the sample sits outside a probe's designed band.
